I'm seeing the same issue, using a single domain.  Tried in Safari and Chrome, using results from Chrome here.

Looking at it in the debugger, it looks like it _might_ be a webpack problem?

[`views/integrationPipeline/index.tsx`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/5b5631049d8ce108da6146676347a83b0c97403b/static/app/views/integrationPipeline/index.tsx#L2C1-L4C1) does a:

```
  const {init} = await import('./init');
  init();
```

where it's correctly expecting to get the `init` function from [`views/integrationPipeline/init.tsx`](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/5b5631049d8ce108da6146676347a83b0c97403b/static/app/views/integrationPipeline/init.tsx#L3).  That calls `initializePipelineView(window.__initialData)`.

But the next frame I see on the call stack is `initializePipelineView`, and it's being called with no arguments.  I am woefully unfamiliar with how webpack functions under the hood, but it smells like webpack is optimizing away that intervening frame, possibly because it thinks `window.__initialData` is empty?  Because Chrome is helpfully pulling the source map, and I can place breakpoints everywhere _but_ in `views/integrationPipeline/init.tsx`.  I can't follow the minimized js enough to tell, either.

Incase anyone comes across this case, 

While this feature is being evaluated, there's a workaround that works when your events contain full file paths in the abs_path field (common in .NET Framework applications).

When this applies:
Your stack frames include abs_path values like:
C:\GitHub\MyRepo\ProjectA\Services\Foo.cs
C:\GitHub\MyRepo\ProjectB\Services\Foo.cs

Configuration:
Create separate code mappings using the full path as the Stack Trace Root:

Stack Trace Root                             |          Source Code Root

C:\GitHub\MyRepo\ProjectA\          |                ProjectA/
C:\GitHub\MyRepo\ProjectB\          |                ProjectB/

Why it works:
Sentry's matching logic checks abs_path.startswith(stack_root), so the full paths distinguish between projects even when the relative filename paths are identical.

Caveats:
Requires consistent build paths across environments
You must delete any existing empty stack_root mapping first (empty string matches everything)
Moving this ticket into our [Improve Code Mappings project](https://linear.app/getsentry/project/improve-code-mappings-e15bd956a087/issues)
Another example of this contained within internal ticket [#173402](https://sentry.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/173402)

@ceorourke Marking the issue as `Archive until escalating` option and then escalating it does trigger the alert. 

Marking as archived until it affects a certain number of users or by time does not result in the alert triggering, but in both these cases the issue is marked as "Ongoing" instead of "Escalating". I don't expect the alert to trigger.

Hi, I created the original support ticket that led to this issue.

In my dashboard when I archive until it happens one more time and it does happen one more time, it is displayed as "Escalating".

What is the expected way to use sentry to get a notification the next time an error is triggered ?
@ceorourke @leedongwei , can you confirm the expected behaviour above?

I looked into this and the expected behavior is that this filter only triggers when you've selected the default "archive until escalating" option. However, if you have workflow notifications enabled you'll receive a notification for this without setting up an alert rule. Here's a screenshot from my test app I ran this in. I did the same setup where I archived the issue until it happened one more time from now, sent another event, and received this email: The [evaluation criteria for this filter](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/master/src/sentry/rules/conditions/reappeared_event.py#L17) is simple - we check if the event state `has_escalated` is True. In post process we only set `has_escalated` to True in 2 situations - if the issue was set to "archive until escalating" and a new event has come in ([here](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/master/src/sentry/tasks/post_process.py#L833)) or if a [new issue is escalating](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/master/src/sentry/tasks/post_process.py#L1520). As a follow up I think we can add the notification I put a screenshot of to the [workflow notification documentation](https://docs.sentry.io/product/alerts/notifications/#workflow-notifications) and look into the issue state being marked as "escalating" in this scenario - in my opinion a single issue coming in isn't "escalating".

@ceorourke In that case, the UI should not set the issue as "Escalated" in the activity tab and "Escalating" in the issues feed after the "Archive until it happens once" action. Because the UI is telling me "this issue went from archived to escalating" I expect the alert to trigger, but the alert did not detect it. This inconsistency is the cause of this issue.
I've made a ticket for our backlog to address the issue substatus in this instance, thanks for the report!

Hey @ceorourke, A customer ran into the same problem.
The WHEN trigger looks for "Archived to Escalating" However this is only triggered if Sentry's Escalating Algoritm is firing.
Under the hood I found 2 flags: has_reappeared &  has_escalated
The first one is changed in the case when you manually set a condition like when 10 users or 1 single event.
But the has_escalated flag only is changed when Sentry uses it's ML/forecasting to predict escalation.

The alert at this moment is not triggering because has_escalated is still false.

I think we need to improve this behaviour and also update the has_escalated flag to true if there are manual rules the users wants to escalate this from
@ceorourke another user has reported the [same issue here](https://sentry.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/164935).
Ok, we'll take a look.

Btw, I thought a little on this: 
From a user perspective they think the Archive until x (every option outside of escalating) means that once this happens it's escalating in their perception. But the main trigger is the is_escalated flag which is set by Sentry and not the user/manual.
So maybe the ask here is to have an alert trigger that looks for has_reappeared or issues will be manually escalating but that seems more of a breaking change. 
TLDR: I think it's working as expected but the perception of the customers are different + there is no replacement to get what the customer wants. (getting alerts when their manual archived until X is triggered)
As mentioned [above](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/issues/97778#issuecomment-3225555905), we have a ticket in the backlog to address this confusion with archiving, thanks for looking into it!

Just re-iterating for all that we're tracking a backlog item to change how the UI sets the "issue as "Escalated" in the activity tab and "Escalating" in the issues feed after the "Archive until it happens once" action". It's possible this should be "ongoing" instead we still need to make that determination however.

Please note it is the intended behaviour that that "archive until happens x times" does not modify the issue state to be `has_escalated`.

It's worth mentioning that this seems to be a **regression**. 

Our alerts used to be set up long before Sentry added the "archive until escalated" option. And they used to fire when issues were breaching the set up threshold. However, after certain update they all stopped.

It's also worth mentioning that sometimes setting a strict threshold over a number of events or affected users is preferred to non-determenistic "until escalated" approach. This gives monitoring people more flexibility and allow them to react quicker if things go completely wrong. Thus being able to setup an alert for this type of transition is essential.

Given all this, can it be prioritized higher?

Closing the loop on this thread and some investigation:
- when[ we moved from "ignored" to "archived"](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/pulls?page=5&q=is%3Apr+is%3Aclosed+archived)
- we changed the issue alert trigger from "ignored to unresolved" to "archived to escalating" (see docs here: https://web.archive.org/web/20210610170040/https://docs.sentry.io/product/alerts-notifications/issue-alerts/#triggers)
- this left a gap where some cases that would have alerted in the past cannot be alerted on now - specifically because of the expected behavior that Colleen has outlined above. 
- we're going to look into changing anything that is currently marked as "escalating" in the UI to be treated as escalated for the purposes of alerting to close this gap

Note: this will result in more alerts firing than in the past 2.5 years

What happens when moving away from a Lambda function that was originally instrumented via the integration to manually upgrading and managing the lambda layer

1. Created a new org and new project in Sentry

9. Error and trace were still sent correctly

I took a look at this from the SDK-side and I think we can easily add the timing values for resource spans. For TTFB of resources, ~we can simply take the `entry.responseStart` value as [documented here](https://web.dev/articles/ttfb#measure-resource-requests)~ (see [comment](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/issues/63739#issuecomment-3299293235) below). This value should already contain all the timing information (i.e. request lifecycle phases) required to deliver a TTFB value for resources. 

The caveat is that we'll only get correct `responseStart` values for resources fetched from the same origin as the requested page or for resources from 3rd parties that send a valid `Timing-Allow-Origin` header in their response.  [See here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/PerformanceResourceTiming/responseStart#value).

Anyway, I think from the SDK perspective, we'll simply attach responseStart values as a span attribute to the resource spans. The product can then work with this information and display some kind of augmentation that this value denotes the TTFB of this resource. My only ask is that we don't confuse TTFB of resources with the page TTFB (for web vitals). 

While we're at it, we might as well add some other timing values. I'll open a PR with some more details once we figured them out.

I believe there's an easy part to this and a hard part:

1. Improving the outcome reason from `filtered-transaction` to the pattern that was applied should be easy. We can migrate health check filters to [generic inbound filters](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/09d75973b9da642307ea0135ced5966c991ebf38/src/sentry/ingest/inbound_filters.py#L384-L388) and use something like `health-check-pattern:*heartbeat*` as an outcome reason, which would still be low-cardinality.
2. Keeping track of discarded samples is a harder problem. After all, we discard these transactions because we _don't_ want to store them. This would involve setting up a separate data channel to communicate discards from outer relays inwards, and some form of storage to hold them (redis?). I would advice against this because of the implied complexity.

Will discuss with the team if we can implement (1), or if a different team is better suited to make the changes.

Hi @melv-n and @adnweedon, after some more investigation, I have identified the root cause of this behavior.

Specifically, Sentry CLI 3.0.0 now creates releases using a newer API endpoint. It seems that this new endpoint only allows users to create releases for projects which they are members of; I think this restriction is itself the underlying bug, since the restriction is not present on the still available legacy API endpoint that Sentry CLI 2.x and older were using. The error you are observing is [raised when you hit this supposed permissions error](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/afa2147de3166909debe86a3805c9101bdd0b8be/src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_releases.py#L706-L718).

I am going to transfer this issue to the backend's repo, since it makes more sense to fix this bug in the backend than the CLI.

### My recommendation for you

This permissions error should only occur if you are using a [Personal Token](https://docs.sentry.io/account/auth-tokens/#personal-tokens); however, for security reasons, we **recommend avoiding personal tokens in CI environments**.

Therefore, I would recommend you reconfigure your CI environment to use an [Organization Token](https://docs.sentry.io/account/auth-tokens/#organization-tokens), instead. These tokens are specifically designed to be used in CI environments, and should have the permissions to create releases for any projects in your org. Switching to an org token is both best practice security-wise and should also allow you to work around this bug.

I would like to add a +1 here too; we use a misbehaving chat plugin on our site, and CSP reports for that plugin have just accumulated to 83k reports. Not only does this start to threaten our quota, it's also (as Scott said) drowning out other issues.

I understand this is causing headaches with regards to the business model, but I would advocate for an option to drop report requests on the Sentry side without incurring charges. CSP violations quickly stagger up, and the only sensible thing for us to do is turn them off entirely to avoid spending our budget on pointless issues, which cannot be the right way to solve this.  
Now that I think of it, this would even allow for a possible attack scenario: If an attacker figures out a CSP report URI points to Sentry, they can first cause millions of CSP violations until the victim's quota must be exceeded, and then work undisturbed while Sentry is "blinded" until the billing period concedes. Sure this is a little contrived, but still imaginable.

We have reached the point where we’re considering moving our CSP reporting away from Sentry, due to the fact that CSP errors are treated the same as application errors and both come out of the same Sentry quota.

I won’t relitigate the arguments for allowing filtering or sampling of CSP errors as they are detailed above, but I do think that they should be given a separate usage quota so that an influx of CSP errors won’t stop ALL errors from being monitored.

There is a fundamental difference between application errors and CSP errors, in that application errors are (generally speaking) *actionable* by the developer. Fixing a bug, improving validation or refactoring code to be more defensive are all options to reduce the number of errors reported. The aspirational (but probably unachievable) goal is zero errors.

But CSP errors are not actionable, as they generally represent attempts at doing something that the developer has strictly forbidden by policy. Once a policy has been fine tuned to only allow the exact sources and all false positives have been addressed, there is nothing further the developer can do. There is no aspirational target of zero CSP errors. CSP errors are to be expected.

Having these two different classes of errors come out the same Sentry quota makes it impractical for us to continue with CSP reporting via Sentry. We hope that in future this changes.

For the benefit of others looking for a solution to filtering CSP noise from Sentry without either
1. relaxing your CSP strictness, or
2. turning off CSP reporting entirely

...we are exploring a solution that uses a combination of `Content-Security-Policy` and `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` headers to maintain a strict policy, but at the same time control which violations will be reported to Sentry.

For example, one of the noisiest CSP violations that we see is `Blocked 'font' from 'data:'`.  That is:
```
effective_directive  font-src
blocked_uri          data
```

One of the biggest culprits for these violations seems to be browser extensions. For example, the Grammarly browser extension is one that we see commonly in traces where this violation occurred.

The relevant part of our policy currently looks something like this:
```http
Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com; report-uri <sentry uri here>
``` 

(Note that `data:` is not a permitted `font-src`, nor do we wish to allow it.)

Ideally, we want to continue blocking attempts to load fonts from data URIs, but equally given the volume of such violations, we want to stop sending them to Sentry so that they don't consume our entire error quote (accepting that, in doing so, we lose visibility of these violations).

To achieve this, we can change our policy headers as follows:
```diff
- Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com; report-uri <sentry uri here>
+ Content-Security-Policy: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com;
+ Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com data:; report-uri <sentry uri here>
```

First, remove `report-uri` from your _actual_ policy.  Everything else remains the same, so you're still blocking the same violations, but nothing will be reported to Sentry (yet).

Next, add a new `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` header that is _exactly the same as your actual policy_, but also:
* includes report-uri for reporting violations to Sentry
* includes `data:` in the `font-src` directive  (and any others that you want to exclude from Sentry)
 
I hope this helps anyone in the same situation, struggling with Sentry's decision to combine application-level errors and CSP errors into a single quota.

@mologie Hello! Thanks for the detailed feedback.

I'm unfamiliar with Keycloak - do they have a concept of Groups? 

The usual implementation to limit user access to applications would be: 

1. create a group (e.g. Engineering group)
2. put the relevant users to that group (you and your teammates, but not Mike the Janitor)
3. assign an application (e.g. Sentry, Github, etc) to that group only

It ensures that the identity provider (Keycloak/Okta/AzureAD/etc) would enforce that assignment and it will not provide Mike credentials to "talk" to Sentry at all. This is important as Sentry (or another app with overzealous tracking) would not have the chance to know that Mike is in your organization and read his profile data from the provider. 

Hopefully this helps! Please let me know if this is/isn't doable with Keycloak.

@leedongwei Hello! Thank you for your response and suggestion.

Okta seems to implement these groups indeed where it fails the authentication process when a user is not assigned to an application. This is useful in practice, but definitely non-standard behavior that is not covered by SAML in general.

Keycloak takes a rather pure (but as you can see from my issue not necessarily practical) approach to SAML: It authenticates the user, It may also pass authorization statements. However, the evaluation of authentication and authorization information must be done be the SP (here: Sentry).

My point is handled in the SAML 2 Technical Overview document page 12 [1]:

> In a SAML-enabled deployment, when they subsequently attempt toaccess a protected resource at the SP, the SP will send the user to the IdP with an authentication requestin order to have the user log in. Thus this scenario is referred to as SP-initiated web SSO. Once logged in,the IdP can produce an assertion that can be used by the SP to validate the user's access rights to theprotected resource.

Let's also compare to GitLab, a common source code management platform, which enables the administrator to configure groups/assertions (passed by e.g. Keycloak after SSO) that are allowed to access GitLab:

https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/integration/saml.html#required-groups

GitLab enables not only to define which assertions/groups are allowed to access the repository, but also enables to define who is global instance administrator. Sentry could adopt similar behavior by assigning the user to the right organization role (user, manager, admin, etc.) right away instead of requiring manual intervention by an admin after the user first signed in.

Regarding your privacy point:

> This is important as Sentry (or another app with overzealous tracking) would not have the chance to know that Mike is in your organization and read his profile data from the provider.

This is not a problem with Keycloak (or any SAML IdP I know of): You still define trusted applications (just like with e.g. Okta), and only those may attempt to retrieve the user profile. Depending on application settings, the user may also have the option to confirm/reject whether the application may receive his profile.

[1] https://www.oasis-open.org/committees/download.php/27819/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0-cd-02.pdf

Get-AdfsCertificate -CertificateType token-signing
--note thumbprint from old cert
Get-AdfsCertificate -CertificateType token-decrypting
--note thumbprint from old cert

Set-ADFSProperties -AutocertificateRollover $false
Remove-AdfsCertificate -CertificateType token-decrypting -Thumbprint <old-decrypt-thumbprint>
Remove-AdfsCertificate -CertificateType token-signing -Thumbprint <old-decrypt-thumbprint>
Set-ADFSProperties -AutocertificateRollover $true

@brianthi Hey! Some customers have asked for custom fields support lately. Was there any progress or official answer on whether or not we can support these fields in the future?

Any news on this topic? The situation is similar at our company: we use the Tempo plugin in Jira, so Account is a mandatory custom field for our Jira projects.

The Jira-Sentry integration doesn't work that way. And this problem, in my opinion, cannot be solved by putting in the documentation that Jira custom fields are not supported for integration. A significant number of Jira plugins build on custom fields, and the number of companies that use Jira without any plugins may be quite small.

We recently setup a Jira integration and almost immediately encountered the same issue.

When we attempt to create a (self-hosted) Jira Server 9.12.16 (with Tempo Plugin 18.9.0) issue from (self-hosted) Sentry 25.12.1 where the _Account_ field is required, we get an error:
> (HTTP 400): Account id 'null' is invalid

Even though the field has the correct value - numeric ID of the desired Tempo Account that exists in Jira.

After checking the logs we found out that the value of the Tempo Account field (`customfield_12585` as shown below) is sent to the Jira server as unquoted number which is incorrect, the value should be quoted.
`[INFO] sentry.integrations.jira_server: jira_server.create_issue (organization_id=1 integration_id=3 jira_project='25325' cleaned_data={'summary': 'Test Issue Summary', 'issuetype': {'id': '3'}, 'security': {'id': '10000'}, 'priority': {'id': '5'}, 'description': 'Sentry Issue: [TEST3|https://sentry.local.loc/organizations/local-org/feedback/?referrer=jira_integration&feedbackSlug=test3%3A880&project=8]', 'labels': [], 'customfield_12072': 'P12345678-5483', 'customfield_12585': 285, 'project': {'id': '25325'}})`

Note the following: `'customfield_12585': 285`
Which should be actually: `'customfield_12585': '285'`

First we tried a workaround by quoting the number in the Sentry web form for creating the Jira issue, however that didn't help and only resulted in double quotations as the quoted input was treated as string this time and quoted again (which would be otherwise correct).

Then we tried a quick fix by modifying the following piece of code at our self-hosted Sentry instance:
https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/25.12.1/src/sentry/integrations/jira_server/integration.py#L1062
`-                                v = int(v)`
`+                                v = v`
Which resulted in the Tempo Account request parameter value being correctly quoted and the issue created.

We aren't of course 100% sure if that's the right place to perform that code change, but it at least helped and confirmed out suspicion.
Could you please fix this properly?

@mbarbey sorry this got stale. I'm thinking about how to fix this but can't really find a good solution as even if we encrypt the credentials, we'd still need to make the key available to the app to decrypt on-demand which defeats the purpose.

Am I missing something here?

@BYK I wasn't thinking about a sophisticated solution.
The issue here is about the fact that by simply having access to the database you can get the credentials of a Jira administrator. And we all know well how frequently databases tend to be dumped and published on the web due to security issues somewhere else on websites or servers. And having plain credentials of an administrator directly in the dumps clearly isn't an optimal situation.

I see 2 possible solutions, one very easy and one easy :

## 1. very easy
Simply generating a random key at the installation, storing it in a file somewhere in the project, and using this key to encrypt the credentials before storing it in the database.
This way, if someone want to get the Jira admin credentials, you need both access to the database and the host machine, which can be 2 differents systems.

## 2. easy
Same thing as the 1st option, but the file containing the encryption key is stored somewhere on the OS where the access is limited by users (like the .ssh directory on linux). It would probably be differents paths depending the OS so it might be a little more difficult than the 1st option, but not too much.
And with this option, if you want to find the credentials, you need both access to the database, the hosting machine and logging as the user Sentry is using.

And in both case, when migrating data to a new server, you will need to copy the security file to the new server or reconfigure the Jira plugin.

What do you think about it ?

Check the response and see that `orgRole` is `member` instead of `manager` and that the `role` in team `sentry` is `null` instead of `admin`:

It looks like not setting team role upon invitation is intended though, looking at this comment in the code:

https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/4010c65952d146949058699a03341ac95df089c6/src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_member/index.py#L436-L443

On the other hand, the organization role assignment issue looks like a bug. The organization member is created based on `result["role"]`, which itself is based on the `role` value in the request payload:

https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/4010c65952d146949058699a03341ac95df089c6/src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_member/index.py#L425-L430

although `role` is deprecated: the [endpoint document](https://docs.sentry.io/api/organizations/add-a-member-to-an-organization/) only mentions `orgRole` and we see traces of the deprecation in the code:

https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/4010c65952d146949058699a03341ac95df089c6/src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_member/index.py#L48-L54

A simple fix would be to use the `assigned_org_role` variable when creating the organization member:

https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/blob/4010c65952d146949058699a03341ac95df089c6/src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_member/index.py#L317-L325

Dear Sentry Team,

I wanted to follow up on this issue as it continues to significantly impact our workflows.

Since we initially reported this problem, we have found no viable workaround. The suggested solution of reinstalling the integration under a different user is not feasible for us because it would sever all existing links between Sentry events and GitLab issues. This loss of historical data is unacceptable and would disrupt our issue tracking processes.

The inability to set the issue creator in the GitLab integration means that all issues created via Sentry are attributed to the administrator who set up the integration. 

This misattribution leads to several problems:
- Confusion in Issue Tracking: Team members cannot identify the actual reporters of issues, leading to delays and inefficiencies in addressing them.
- Incorrect Notifications: The administrator receives all notifications for issues they did not create, while the actual creators may miss important updates.
- Inaccurate Reporting: Our metrics and analytics on issue creation and resolution are skewed due to incorrect attribution.
Impact on Our Operations:

This issue has been ongoing for over six months and continues to hinder our team's productivity. Proper attribution of issues is crucial for efficient collaboration and accurate reporting.

We understand that the development team has other priorities, but we kindly ask if there has been any progress on this issue or if it could be reconsidered for prioritization. The resolution of this problem would greatly enhance our use of Sentry in conjunction with GitLab and benefit other users facing similar challenges.

If there are any interim solutions or if there's any way we can assist in testing potential fixes, we would be happy to help.

Thank you for your attention to this matter, and we look forward to any updates you can provide.

@alex-gubernsky we have an in house Jira integration. I was wondering why you don't use that and rely on webhooks?

> [@alex-gubernsky](https://github.com/alex-gubernsky) we have an in house Jira integration. I was wondering why you don't use that and rely on webhooks?

Hi @sentaur-athena,
We use webhooks to export data from Sentry for long-term storage and custom analytics. One of the data points we would like to export during this process is the Jira tickets linked to issues. Currently, the only way to obtain this information is by pulling it via the API — i.e. querying all issue details for each issue — which becomes very inefficient when dealing with a large number of issues and when only a few have linked tickets. 

AFAIR, there is also no `LastUpdated` field available in the issues (or it cannot be used via the API), so we cannot limit queries to only recently updated issues (i.e. those that may have had tickets assigned).

On the other hand, webhooks would be triggered only for those issues that have a linked ticket, making the process much more efficient.

I hope this clarifies things.

## Using Service Accounts

### Prerequisites

- **Create a GitLab service account**:
    - Create a dedicated user account in your GitLab instance for the Sentry integration
    - Grant this service account Maintainer or Owner permissions on the GitLab groups you want to integrate
    - Use this service account for all subsequent steps instead of your personal account

### Configuration Steps

**Note:** You can complete the rest of the steps with any Sentry account with `org:write` permissions

**Note:** You'll need Maintainer or Owner permissions in GitLab. Projects owned by individual users are not supported - only group-owned projects.

1. **Log into GitLab** using your service account (or personal account if not using a service account)
2. **Navigate to your GitLab group settings**:
    - Go to the Settings section of your GitLab group instance
    - In the sidebar, select 'Applications'
    - Or navigate directly to `/-/settings/applications` in your GitLab instance
3. **Create the Sentry application**:
    - Fill out the form with the following information:
        - **Name:** Sentry
        - **Redirect URI:** https://sentry.io/extensions/gitlab/setup/
        - **Scopes:** api
    - Ensure **'Confidential'** is checked
    - Click **Save Application**
4. **Save your credentials**:
    - Copy the **Application ID** and **Secret** from the resulting page
    - You'll need these for the next phase of setup in Sentry

### Important Notes

- If you used a GitLab service account, all integration activities (comments, issue creation, etc.) will be attributed to that service account
- This helps maintain proper access control and prevents disruption when team members leave
- The integration will only work with group-owned projects, not user-owned projects

The next step will be configuring these credentials in your Sentry organization settings.

A GitLab repository service account with suitable credentials cannot complete integration due to SSO/SAML authentication requirements.

## Proposed Solution

Extend Sentry's API to allow programmatic repository integration configuration using Admin accounts or service accounts with proper authentication mechanisms.

### API Capabilities Should Include:

- Adding repositories to Sentry projects programmatically
- Assigning proper repository roles to users in Sentry during the integration process
- Support for service account authentication (API tokens, OAuth, etc.) that doesn't rely on individual user SSO sessions
- Proper validation and error handling to prevent misuse while maintaining security

### Authentication Enhancements:

- Support for long-lived service account tokens that can operate independently of individual user sessions
- API-based authentication that bypasses SSO requirements for automated workflows
- Granular permission scopes that allow repository integration without requiring full administrative privileges

## Expected Benefits

- Enhanced Security: Eliminate dependency on individual users with elevated privileges, reducing single points of failure
- SSO Compatibility: Enable automation in SSO environments where service accounts cannot authenticate through traditional web flows
- Automation Support: Enable API-driven workflows that reduce manual intervention and accelerate setup
- Scalability: Allow large organizations to integrate multiple repositories without process bottlenecks
- DevOps Alignment: Enable self-service capabilities while maintaining security boundaries
- Business Continuity: Ensure integrations remain functional regardless of personnel changes

## Use Case Example

An Observability team wants to set up error monitoring for multiple GitLab repositories across different Sentry projects:

1. The team's service account authenticates via API token (not SSO-dependent)
2. Repository integration is configured programmatically with appropriate scopes
3. Setup scales automatically for new projects without requiring individual admin intervention
4. Integration remains functional even when team members change roles or leave the organization
